subject: Banking
title: Cross-Border Payments on Blockchain
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Cross-Border Payments on Blockchain.

hook.text: Sending $200 from the US to Nigeria through banks costs $14 in fees and takes 3-5 days.

buildup.text: Traditional cross-border payments pass through correspondent banks.

discovery.text: Ripple and Stellar built blockchain networks specifically for cross-border payments.

twist.text: The SEC sued Ripple, calling its XRP token a security.

climax.text: Blockchain can cut remittance costs dramatically. But regulation, not technology, decides when that future arrives.

punchline.text: $14 fees to $0.01. Blockchain payments wait for regulators, not engineers.

quiz.question: What is the main barrier to blockchain adoption in cross-border payments?
options: Regulatory uncertainty and legal challenges like the SEC vs Ripple case

details.summary: Blockchain-based cross-border payments aim to replace the slow, expensive correspondent banking system by settling international transactions on distributed ledgers in minutes rather than days, at a fraction of the current cost.
details.whyItMatters: International payments remain the most expensive and slowest financial transaction type. Blockchain solutions could reduce fees from 6 percent to under 1 percent and settlement from days to minutes for billions of transactions.
takeaways: Traditional cross-border payments take 2 to 5 days and cost 3 to 7 percent
Blockchain solutions can settle in minutes at under 1 percent cost
Regulatory compliance and adoption barriers remain significant challenges

faq.question: Which blockchain platforms are being used for cross-border payments?
faq.answer: Ripple's XRP Ledger, Stellar, and several central bank experiments are the most prominent. JPMorgan's Onyx processes billions in interbank transfers. Stablecoins on various chains also handle a growing volume of cross-border flows.

faq.question: Why haven't blockchain payments replaced SWIFT yet?
faq.answer: Regulatory uncertainty, the need for both sender and receiver to use compatible systems, anti-money-laundering compliance requirements, and institutional resistance from banks benefiting from the current system all slow adoption.
